title: The heart of the Trifid Nebula
caption: The heart of the Trifid Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 20, NGC 6514, Trifid Nebula · constellation Sagittarius
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (AURA/STScI)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: This Hubble image looks into the heart of the Trifid Nebula, cataloged by astronomers as Messier 20 or NGC 6514. It is a well-known region of star formation inside our own Milky Way, lying in the direction of the constellation of Sagittarius.

The nebula owes its name to its appearance in small telescopes. Three bands of dark interstellar dust lie across it, dividing it into three parts. That dust blocks the light of the glowing gas behind it, producing the dark lanes.

In a star-forming region like this, clouds of gas and dust collapse to form new stars, and the energetic light of those young stars in turn makes the surrounding gas glow. Hubble's camera recorded this glow through separate filters for oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, each isolating light from a single gas. Separating them this way helps astronomers map the conditions across the nebula and see how young stars are shaping it.
scale: The Trifid Nebula lies about 9,000 light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, using narrow filters for oxygen, hydrogen-alpha and sulfur. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate light from individual gases, so the colors map chemistry rather than what an eye would see.
